title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: The True Story of BlacKkKlansman
summary: Summer Movie Playlist replay of the SYSK episode on the true story behind Spike Lee's film BlacKkKlansman. Hosts discuss Colorado Springs police detective Ron Stallworth, who in 1978-79 infiltrated the Ku Klux Klan by phone and through fellow detective Chuck Waite, who attended meetings in person. They cover the Klan's history in Colorado and Denver, Stallworth's phone friendship with David Duke, the staged lunch with Duke, the investigation's results (prevented cross burnings, Klan members at NORAD), the film's embellishments, Boots Riley's criticism and Spike Lee's response, and listener mail about table tennis.

segments.title: Summer movie playlist intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Summer Movie Playlist and says this is a replay of the episode on BlacKkKlansman.

segments.title: Opening banter on the film
segments.summary: Hosts discuss having seen the movie, its ending, and a screening in Perth, and praise Spike Lee and John David Washington.

segments.title: Film awards and John David Washington
segments.summary: They note the film's Oscar nominations and Grand Prize at Cannes, and that John David Washington was a college and NFL-Europe football player.

segments.title: Ron Stallworth's career
segments.summary: Ron Stallworth became the first African American officer in Colorado Springs Police Department, joining as a cadet at 19 and being sworn in as an officer on his 21st birthday. He later worked undercover for about thirty years.

segments.title: Klan history in Colorado and Denver
segments.summary: Overview of the three waves of the Klan, and its deep control of Colorado in the 1920s, including Denver officials who were Klan members and the Klan-backed police chief.

segments.title: Stokely Carmichael and the film's invented love interest
segments.summary: Stallworth attended a Stokely Carmichael rally undercover, and the character Patrice was invented for the film.

segments.title: Newspaper ad and the first letter
segments.summary: Stallworth answered a Klan classified ad in October 1978, writing a letter under his real name, expecting only pamphlets.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Short placeholder break in the episode before the discussion resumes.

segments.title: Phone contact with Ken O'Dell
segments.summary: Ken O'Dell called Stallworth's undercover line and invited him to meet. Stallworth drew on his own experiences with racism growing up in El Paso.

segments.title: Chuck Waite as the in-person officer
segments.summary: Stallworth recruited white detective Chuck Waite, who went to meetings in person while wearing a wire.

segments.title: Klan membership and David Duke contact
segments.summary: Waite was admitted to the Klan and received a membership card. Stallworth called Klan national headquarters, where he talked with David Duke, Grand Wizard, about his application.

segments.title: David Duke's political career
segments.summary: Hosts clarify Duke's political background: Louisiana state representative, runs for Democratic and Republican presidential primaries, and an endorsement of Donald Trump.

segments.title: Charlottesville and Jasper Pääkkönen casting
segments.summary: Hosts note Duke's role at the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, which the film uses footage from, and discuss the actor who played Duke.

segments.title: Phone friendship with David Duke
segments.summary: Stallworth and Duke had cordial phone conversations over about nine months that drifted into racism. Stallworth tested Duke with a pronunciation question, and Duke did not suspect him.

segments.title: Staged lunch with Duke
segments.summary: Duke visited Colorado Springs for lunch. Stallworth was assigned to guard him while Chuck Waite was also present, and a photo was taken, which Waite later lost.

segments.title: Motives and results of the investigation
segments.summary: The operation was intelligence gathering, not a takedown. Investigators prevented three cross burnings and identified Klan members at NORAD, and found plots including a bombing of a gay nightclub and theft of weapons from an Army base. The film's bomb plot was invented.

segments.title: Ending of the operation and lack of arrests
segments.summary: The operation ended when Stallworth was nominated to lead the Colorado Springs Klan chapter. Hosts discuss why no arrests were made, and Stallworth's pride in protecting children from cross burnings.

segments.title: The voice discrepancy and the real ending
segments.summary: Stallworth once covered a voice difference by claiming a sinus infection. Stallworth never revealed his identity to Duke, unlike the film's ending.

segments.title: Boots Riley criticism and Spike Lee response
segments.summary: Boots Riley criticized the film on Twitter, arguing it overstated the Black Power and law enforcement relationship and that Stallworth worked for COINTELPRO. Stallworth responded, and Spike Lee later commented on cops in general.

segments.title: Recommendation and disclaimer
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the film and state the episode is not an ad.

segments.title: Table tennis listener mail
segments.summary: A listener, a table tennis coach, corrects hosts on racket sides, pips, and the term choppers versus chiselers from a previous episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for feedback and give contact information.
